newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya calls for international force for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Kenya calls for international force for Zaire.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi called on Wednesday for an international buffer force to be sent to eastern Zaire to cut it off from neighbouring states to the east.

Diplomats said that Moi was effectively adding his weight to Zairean accusations that troops from its eastern neighbours Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi were crossing into eastern Zaire and fighting alongside rebels.

State radio said Moi appealed to the United Nations, United States and European Union to provide a neutral buffer force to "reduce the senseless bloodshed in the region" and allow a peace process to continue.

Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda deny sending troops into Zaire to fight alongside rebels who have seized control of a swath of territory in the east since October and blunted a government army counter-offensive.

Mohamed Sahnoun, the first joint envoy of the United Nations and Organisation of African Unity, arrived on Tuesday in Nairobi, headquarters for his new mission to bring peace to the Great Lakes region.

Since his appointment, Sahnoun has spoken of the need for a comprehensive solution to the Great Lakes crises. But U.N. officials say he will need to tackle problems one by one before political conditions are suitable for an overall resolution.

Moi, whose government has at times poor relations with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, last Friday urged countries that he said were directly involved in the east Zaire war to stop. He did not name any of the states involved.
He called for respect for the territorial integrity of Zaire and urged Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsi rebels to address their grievances against the Zaire government through peaceful means.
Moi, chairman of a group of African heads of state charged with helping end conflict in the Great Lakes region, said Zairean rebels should observe an immediate ceasefire and withdraw.
Calls by two summits of African leaders for a ceasefire in Zaire have been ignored and Kinshasa has rejected negotiations with the rebels, who launched their revolt in October.
The European Commission last week invited Moi and President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda for talks about the war in Zaire.
The two do not see eye-to-eye on the situation in the Great Lakes region and have also been at odds on other matters such as Rwanda, when Uganda backed Tutsi rebels who took power in 1994.
